claims.sentence: Diabetes is a condition in which there is too much glucose, a type of sugar, in the blood.
claims.evidence: Plain general definition; not quoted in retrieved text.

claims.sentence: Both type 1 and type 2 involve insulin, the hormone that helps glucose move out of the blood and into the body's cells.
claims.evidence: Retrieved text says type 1 destroys insulin-making cells and type 2 means too little insulin or insulin that works poorly; the glucose-into-cells mechanism was not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: Both type 1 and type 2 involve insulin, a hormone made by cells in the pancreas.

claims.sentence: The two types share several symptoms: increased thirst, passing urine more often, tiredness and weight loss.
claims.evidence: NHS lists feeling thirsty all the time, peeing more than usual, feeling very tired and losing weight without trying; 111 Wales type 1 lists the same.

claims.sentence: The difference lies in why the problem arises and how it is managed.
claims.evidence: NHS/Diabetes UK differences: cause (immune attack vs too little/poorly working insulin) and treatment differ.

claims.sentence: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition.
claims.evidence: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition; the immune system attacks the cells in the pancreas that make insulin.

claims.sentence: The immune system destroys the cells in the pancreas that make insulin, so the body makes little or no insulin.
claims.evidence: Immune system attacks and destroys insulin-producing cells; 'little or no insulin' not in retrieved text.
claims.newSentence: The immune system attacks and destroys the cells in the pancreas that make insulin.

claims.sentence: It usually develops over days to weeks, particularly in children.
claims.evidence: Symptoms usually develop very quickly in young people (over a few days or weeks); 'children' is narrower than 'young people'.
claims.newSentence: In young people the symptoms usually develop very quickly, over a few days or weeks.

claims.sentence: In adults it can take a few months to appear.
claims.evidence: In adults, the symptoms often take longer to develop (a few months).
claims.newSentence: In adults, the symptoms often take longer to develop, sometimes a few months.

claims.sentence: Type 2 diabetes is not an autoimmune condition.
claims.evidence: Not stated in retrieved text; type 2 described as too little insulin or insulin that does not work well.

claims.sentence: Either the body does not make enough insulin, or the insulin it makes does not work as well as it should.
claims.evidence: Type 2: body makes too little insulin or the insulin it produces does not work as well as it should.

claims.sentence: Diabetes UK lists age, family history, ethnicity and weight among the risk factors.
claims.evidence: Your age, family history, ethnicity, waist circumference and living with obesity or overweight are all risk factors for type 2.

claims.sentence: Type 2 usually develops gradually over years, and it is often picked up at a routine check-up rather than because of obvious symptoms.
claims.evidence: NHS: signs may not be so obvious, condition develops slowly over years. Routine check-up detection not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: Type 2 develops slowly over a period of years, so the signs may not be obvious.

claims.sentence: Type 1 diabetes is treated with insulin, which is needed for life, alongside monitoring of blood glucose.
claims.evidence: Type 1 is treated with insulin for the rest of your life, and regularly checking blood glucose.

claims.sentence: Type 2 diabetes is usually managed first through diet, physical activity and weight management.
claims.evidence: Type 2 managed with lifestyle changes (eating healthily, exercising, trying to lose weight) and sometimes medicines; 'first' not stated.
claims.newSentence: Type 2 diabetes is managed with lifestyle changes such as eating healthily, exercising and trying to lose weight, and sometimes with medicines.

claims.sentence: Medicine may be added if needed, such as metformin, and some people also need insulin.
claims.evidence: Sometimes medicines, such as metformin or insulin.

claims.sentence: The clinician looking after the person decides which treatment is right, and the plan can change over time.
claims.evidence: Not in retrieved text.

claims.sentence: Diabetes UK says neither type currently has a permanent cure.
claims.evidence: Diabetes UK says there isn't a cure for diabetes right now; 'permanent' and 'neither type' not stated.
claims.newSentence: Diabetes UK says there is no cure for diabetes at the moment.

claims.sentence: Type 2 diabetes can sometimes be put into remission, and it can sometimes be prevented.
claims.evidence: NHS-affiliated text: type 2 can sometimes be prevented or put back with lifestyle changes; review describes type 2 remission (HbA1c below diagnostic level for 6 months without glucose-lowering medicine).

claims.sentence: Remission does not mean the condition has gone for good, which is why regular checks are still part of care.
claims.evidence: Review: people in remission still need regular follow-up; condition can return.

claims.sentence: Blood tests are used to diagnose and monitor diabetes.
claims.evidence: Diagnosis by blood glucose/HbA1c tests; monitoring by regularly checking blood glucose.

claims.sentence: The site's pages on blood glucose and on HbA1c explain what they show, and the laboratory report shows the reference range used.
claims.evidence: Harmless pointer to other site pages; no figures given.

claims.sentence: A GP appointment is the route for anyone who has the symptoms above, or who is worried about their risk of type 2 diabetes.
claims.evidence: 111 Wales: visit your GP as soon as possible with the main symptoms; for children contact GP urgently or NHS 111 Wales; call 999 for very drowsy/confused child. Risk-worry route not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: See a GP as soon as possible if you have the main symptoms of diabetes; for a child, contact the GP practice urgently or use NHS 111 if unsure what to do.

claims.sentence: The NHS website sets out the symptoms to look for.
claims.evidence: NHS symptoms pages exist for type 1 and type 2.

claims.sentence: In type 1 diabetes the immune system destroys the cells that make insulin, so the body makes little or no insulin.
claims.evidence: As c06.
claims.newSentence: In type 1 diabetes the immune system attacks and destroys the cells that make insulin.

claims.sentence: In type 2 diabetes the body makes too little insulin or the insulin it makes does not work well.
claims.evidence: As c10.

claims.sentence: Type 1 usually develops over days to weeks, while type 2 usually develops gradually over years.
claims.evidence: Days/weeks is for young people; adults a few months.
claims.newSentence: Type 1 often develops quickly, especially in young people, while type 2 develops slowly over years.

claims.sentence: Type 1 is treated with insulin, with blood glucose monitoring; type 2 is usually managed first with diet, activity and weight management.
claims.evidence: 'first' not backed (see c14).
claims.newSentence: Type 1 is treated with insulin and blood glucose checks; type 2 is managed with lifestyle changes and sometimes medicines.

claims.sentence: Neither type has a permanent cure, although type 2 can sometimes be put into remission.
claims.evidence: See c17.
claims.newSentence: There is no cure for diabetes at the moment, although type 2 can sometimes go into remission.

claims.sentence: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition treated with insulin; type 2 develops when the body makes too little insulin or it works poorly.

notes: Searches 2 and 4 partly returned non-allowed domains (PMC); only the PMC remission review was used. The 111 Wales type 1 page and nhs.uk pages were attributed via search excerpts, not full text. Type 1 onset in children vs 'young people' wording follows 111 Wales. 'Neither type' cure wording and routine-check-up detection were not retrieved.
